lessons.title: Resources and Classification

activities.prompt: Why isn't everything in nature automatically a resource for us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a resource?
activities.body: Look around you. Water, soil, forests and even human skill can help you live well. Anything in your environment that meets your needs is a resource, but only if it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable. People use technology and institutions to turn materials from nature into resources. We can sort resources by origin, exhaustibility, ownership and status of development.
keyPoints: A resource meets our needs and is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable.
Human beings transform materials from the environment into resources and use them.
Resources can be classified by origin, exhaustibility, ownership and status of development.
Resources are vital for human survival and for maintaining the quality of life.
activities.explanation: Resources are not free gifts of nature. People and their tools turn materials into useful things.

activities.prompt: A huge rock sits on a hill near Anu's village. No machine in the village can cut it. People also do not want to build with it. Anu asks: is this rock a resource?
steps: A resource must be something we can actually use, so the rock must pass three tests.
No machine can cut the rock, so it is not technologically accessible yet.
People do not want it, so it is not culturally acceptable either.
So the rock is not a resource now, but it could become one if technology and people's choices change.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: On the basis of origin, resources are divided into biotic and ______ resources.
activities.hint: It starts with 'a' and means non-living.
activities.explanation: Origin means where a resource comes from. Biotic comes from living things and abiotic from non-living things.

activities.prompt: On the basis of exhaustibility, how are resources classified?
options: Biotic and abiotic
Individual and community
Renewable and non-renewable
Potential and reserves
activities.explanation: Exhaustibility asks whether a resource can run out. So we get renewable and non-renewable resources.

activities.prompt: Match each basis of classification with its two or more types.
activities.explanation: Well done! Each basis sorts resources in its own way. Remember all four bases.

activities.prompt: Put these types of resources in the order given in your book, on the basis of status of development.
items: Potential
Developed stock
Reserves
activities.explanation: On the basis of status of development, the lesson lists potential first, then developed stock, then reserves.

activities.prompt: Why do human beings create institutions?
options: To live apart from nature
To avoid using technology
To slow down economic development
To accelerate economic development
activities.explanation: People interact with nature through technology and create institutions to speed up economic development. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: A huge rock sits on a mountain. No machine can cut or lift it. People also do not want to use it. Is this rock a resource?
options: Yes, because it is a useful part of nature.
Yes, because all natural things are resources.
No, because it fails the tests for a resource.
No, because rocks can never become resources.

why.Yes, because it is a useful part of natu: Thinks usefulness alone is enough, but all three conditions must hold.
why.Yes, because all natural things are reso: Believes nature gives resources freely, but conditions must be met.
why.No, because rocks can never become resou: Thinks rocks can never be resources, but technology can change that.

activities.explanation: Correct: it is not accessible by technology and not acceptable, so not a resource yet.

activities.prompt: Grandfather says, 'River water is a free gift of nature.' The village paid for pipes, a pump, and a worker. Is grandfather right?
options: Yes, because the river itself was made by nature.
Yes, because water is free for every living thing.
No, because people worked hard to make water usable.
No, because water is not a natural thing.

why.Yes, because the river itself was made b: Thinks a natural origin makes it free, but human work matters.
why.Yes, because water is free for every liv: Confuses water being shared in nature with being a ready resource.
why.No, because water is not a natural thing: Wrongly thinks water is not natural; the issue is human work.

activities.explanation: Correct: human effort and tools turned water into a usable resource.

activities.prompt: Long ago, people saw sunlight but could not store its power. Today, solar panels turn sunlight into electricity for homes. What changed sunlight into a resource?
options: Sunlight became stronger over the years.
People learned new skills and built new tools.
Sunlight changed its own form into electricity.
The sun moved closer to the earth.

Thinks nature changed, but sunlight stayed the same.
why.Sunlight changed its own form into elect: Thinks sunlight changed itself; people changed how it is used.
Thinks the sun's position changed, which is not the cause.

activities.explanation: Correct: human activity and technology made sunlight usable.

activities.prompt: Meera sorts things into two boxes. Box one: rice, fish, wood. Box two: wind, water, stones. Which rule is she using to sort?
options: Things that can finish and things that cannot.
Things that come from life and things that do not.
Things owned by one person and things owned by all.
Things we use now and things we save for later.

why.Things that can finish and things that c: Confuses origin with exhaustibility; wind and water can also finish in a sense.
why.Things owned by one person and things ow: Confuses origin with ownership; nothing here is about who owns them.
why.Things we use now and things we save for: Confuses origin with status of development; nothing here is about saving.

activities.explanation: Correct: rice, fish and wood are biotic; wind, water and stones are abiotic.

activities.prompt: Village A makes power from wind. Village B makes power from coal. After fifty years, B must buy power from A. Why did this happen?
options: Village A's wind became stronger over the years.
Village B used up coal, which cannot be renewed.
Village B's people moved away and left no workers.
Village A's machines were newer and worked faster.

why.Village A's wind became stronger over th: Thinks wind supply changed; wind renews and stays usable.
why.Village B's people moved away and left n: Thinks people left; the problem is the coal finishing.
why.Village A's machines were newer and work: Thinks it is about machine speed; the real cause is exhaustibility.

activities.explanation: Correct: coal is non-renewable, so it gets used up.

activities.prompt: Engineers find oil deep under the sea. No machine can reach it yet. Ten years later, they build one and pump the oil. What was the oil before?
options: It was a reserve saved for future use.
It was a developed stock already in use.
It was a potential resource waiting for technology.
It was an individual resource owned by one person.

Confuses reserve with potential; a reserve is saved on purpose.
Confuses developed stock with potential; nothing was in use yet.
why.It was an individual resource owned by o: Confuses status of development with ownership; no owner is mentioned.

activities.explanation: Correct: it existed but needed technology to become usable.

lessons.title: Sustainable Development and Global Summits

activities.prompt: Why did over 100 world leaders fly to Rio in 1992?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Development That Lasts
activities.body: Imagine spending your pocket money so fast that nothing is left for tomorrow. Sustainable development means growth without damaging the environment. It also saves enough for future generations. Long ago, people treated resources as free gifts and used them carelessly. This careless use led to global ecological crises. So in June 1992, over 100 leaders met at Rio de Janeiro. They adopted Agenda 21 for global sustainable development.
keyPoints: Development should not damage the environment.
Today's growth must not rob future generations.
The 1992 Rio Summit adopted Agenda 21 for sustainable development.
activities.explanation: Use resources with care today, so tomorrow's children have them too.

activities.prompt: Riya's town cuts trees fast to sell wood. Her little brother asks: will there be wood for him when he grows up? What is the problem here?
steps: The town wants money now, so it cuts trees very fast.
But trees grow slowly, so fast cutting empties the forest.
The town gains today, but her brother may get no wood later.
So development that harms nature also hurts future people, and that is not sustainable.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does sustainable economic development mean?
options: Development that damages the environment
Development without damaging the environment
Development that ignores future generations
activities.explanation: Well done! It grows without harming nature and keeps resources for tomorrow.

activities.prompt: Long ago, many people thought resources were free gifts of nature.
activities.explanation: Yes. Because they seemed free, people used them without any care.

activities.prompt: In June ______, more than 100 heads of state met at Rio de Janeiro.
activities.hint: Think of the year of the first International Earth Summit.
activities.explanation: The first International Earth Summit was held at Rio de Janeiro in June 1992.

activities.prompt: What did the leaders sign at the Rio Summit?
options: A rule to cut down more forests
A promise to keep resources free forever
A declaration on climatic change and biodiversity
activities.explanation: They signed the Declaration on Global Climatic Change and Biological Diversity.

activities.prompt: Match each Rio idea with its meaning.
pairs: Meeting of over 100 heads of state
A plan for global sustainable development
activities.explanation: Each part of the Rio Summit works towards caring for the Earth.

activities.prompt: Agenda 21 wants only the national government to make a plan.
activities.explanation: Not quite — every local government should draw its own local Agenda 21.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: People thought resources were free gifts of nature
Resources were used up to satisfy the greed of a few
Resources piled up in a few hands
Society split into haves and have-nots
The world faced global ecological crises
activities.explanation: Careless use and greed led to unfair sharing and a global ecological crisis.

activities.prompt: Why did over 100 heads of state meet at the Rio Summit?
options: To divide resources among a few people
To close all factories around the world
To plan a grand sports festival
To discuss environment and development together
activities.explanation: They met to tackle urgent problems of environmental protection and development.

activities.prompt: Long ago, people took as much wood, water and land as they wanted. They thought nature would never run out. Today many resources are almost gone. Why did people use resources so freely?
options: They believed nature's gifts were free and endless
They wanted to save resources for future people
They were told by governments to use more
They did not know how to use resources at all

why.They wanted to save resources for future: This mistake swaps the real belief with the idea we teach today.
why.They were told by governments to use mor: No fact says governments told them; the belief came from their own thinking.
why.They did not know how to use resources a: They did use resources well; the problem was using too much, not using wrongly.

activities.explanation: Right. If a gift seems free and endless, people use it without care.

activities.prompt: A mayor builds a big factory. It gives jobs today, but its smoke harms the air and the river. Which idea of sustainable development does this factory break?
options: Development should not damage the environment
Development should give jobs to many people
Development should be planned by local leaders
Development should be signed at world summits

why.Development should give jobs to many peo: Jobs are good, but the rule being broken is about nature, not jobs.
why.Development should be planned by local l: Local planning is an Agenda 21 idea, not the rule broken here.
why.Development should be signed at world su: Summits are for world leaders, not for one town's factory.

activities.explanation: Right. The smoke damages air and river, so it harms the environment.

lessons.title: Resource Planning and Conservation

activities.prompt: Why do some places have plenty while others run short?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why plan resources?
activities.body: Resources are not spread evenly. Some regions are rich in one thing but poor in another. So India plans how to use them wisely. Planning means listing resources, mapping them, building skills and technology, and linking plans to national goals. If we use too much too fast, people and nature both suffer. Sustainable development means meeting today's needs without harming tomorrow.
keyPoints: Planning helps us use resources wisely
Resources are spread unevenly across regions
Over-use causes problems for people and nature
Sustainable development protects the future
activities.explanation: Careful planning keeps resources useful for everyone, now and later.

activities.prompt: Two villages need water. Village A has many rivers. Village B has almost no water but rich soil. A planner says: 'Send all water plans to Village A. It has more water.' Is this good planning?
steps: Village A already has water, so extra plans there help less.
Village B lacks water, so its rich soil cannot be used fully.
Good planning first finds what each region has and what it lacks.
So the planner should match water plans to Village B's need, not just to A's supply.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sustainable development
activities.body: In 1987, the Brundtland Commission Report introduced the idea of sustainable development. It means using resources so that today's needs are met without spoiling things for the future. India has worked on resource planning since the First Five Year Plan after Independence. Planning early and planning well keeps resources safe for the children of tomorrow too.
keyPoints: The Brundtland Commission Report of 1987 introduced sustainable development
India has planned resources since the First Five Year Plan
Sustainable development thinks about the future
activities.explanation: Sustainable development is like planting a tree whose shade you may never sit in.

activities.prompt: You have one cake and many friends. Why do you cut it carefully instead of grabbing a big piece? Planning resources works the same way. What is planning?
options: A widely accepted strategy for judicious use of resources
A way to use up all resources very quickly
A rule that stops people from using resources
activities.explanation: Planning is the accepted way to use resources wisely, just like sharing the cake fairly.

activities.prompt: Some regions are rich in certain resources but ______ in others.
activities.hint: Think of the opposite of rich.
activities.explanation: No region has everything. Rich in one thing can mean short of another.

activities.prompt: India has enormous diversity in the availability of resources.
activities.explanation: Different parts of India have very different resources. That is why planning matters.

activities.prompt: Match each part of resource planning with what it means.
pairs: Estimating resources in quality and quantity
activities.explanation: Resource planning has clear steps: find, measure, build the set-up, then connect to national goals.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of resource planning in order, from first to last.
items: Identify and inventory resources across regions
Survey, map and estimate the resources
Build a planning structure with technology, skill and institutions
Match resource plans with national development plans
activities.explanation: First find what you have, then measure it, then build the set-up, and finally link it to national plans.

activities.prompt: State X has lots of coal but very little water. State Y has many rivers but little coal. They trade with each other. Why does this trade help both states?
options: Each state fills its own gap using the other's rich resource
Each state wants to sell everything and keep nothing at home
Each state is trying to copy the other state's resources
Each state has too many resources and must throw some away

why.Each state wants to sell everything and: This thinks trade is about greed, not about filling what a region lacks.
why.Each state is trying to copy the other s: This confuses trade with copying; regions cannot create the resources they lack.
why.Each state has too many resources and mu: This thinks richness is a problem; the real issue is the lack in each state.

activities.explanation: Right. Each state is rich in one thing and lacking in the other, so trade balances them.

activities.prompt: A district has fertile soil. But the plan for using it was made without skilled people or proper technology. The soil still stays underused. Which part of resource planning was missing?
options: Surveying and mapping the fertile soil of the district
Matching the soil plan with national development plans
A planning structure with technology, skill and institutions
Making an inventory of soil in all the other districts

why.Surveying and mapping the fertile soil o: The soil was already known and mapped; finding it again would not help use it.
why.Matching the soil plan with national dev: The problem is local execution, not a mismatch with national plans.
why.Making an inventory of soil in all the o: Other districts do not matter here; the failure is in this district's set-up.

activities.explanation: Right. Without technology, skill and institutions, even a good plan cannot work.

activities.prompt: A country plans its resources well, but its plan says nothing about the country's overall national goals. What is the likely result?
options: The resource plan may not fit the country's bigger development path
The country will immediately face irrational consumption of resources
The country will have to survey and map all its resources again
The country will invent the idea of sustainable development itself

why.The country will immediately face irrati: Over-consumption is a separate problem; it is not caused by skipping this matching step.
why.The country will have to survey and map: Surveying was already done; the missing part is matching, not counting.
why.The country will invent the idea of sust: Sustainable development came from the Brundtland Report, not from this planning gap.

activities.explanation: Right. Matching resource plans with national plans is a needed step; skipping it breaks the link.

activities.prompt: A city keeps using its groundwater faster than rain can refill it. Wells dry up. Poor families suffer most, and the land nearby turns barren. What does this situation show?
options: Irrational use of resources causes social and environmental problems
The city needs a bigger inventory of its groundwater resources
The city should wait for the Brundtland Commission to solve it
The city's resource planning started too long before Independence

why.The city needs a bigger inventory of its: The city may know its water well; the problem is how fast it is being used.
why.The city should wait for the Brundtland: The Commission only introduced the idea of sustainable development; it does not fix cities.
why.The city's resource planning started too: The timing of planning is not the issue; the way water is used is the issue.

activities.explanation: Right. Over-using groundwater hurt people (social) and the land (environment), exactly as the fact says.

activities.prompt: Before 1987, planners mostly thought about using resources fast for growth. After the Brundtland Commission Report, planners began asking a new question. Which question fits the new idea?
options: How can we use resources today without harming future generations?
How can we count and map every resource in every region?
How can we start resource planning right after Independence?
How can we match our resource plans with national plans?

why.How can we count and map every resource: Counting and mapping are older planning steps, not the new idea from 1987.
why.How can we start resource planning right: Planning since the First Five Year Plan was already happening before 1987.
why.How can we match our resource plans with: Matching with national plans is an older planning step, not the new 1987 idea.

activities.explanation: Right. Sustainable development means meeting present needs without hurting the future.

lessons.title: Land Resources and Land Utilisation

activities.prompt: How does India decide what each piece of its land should be used for?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Land Matters
activities.body: Land is a precious natural resource. It supports plants, animals, people, farms, transport and communication. But land is limited in size, so we must plan its use with care. India's land comes in different forms: plains, mountains and plateaus. Each form helps us in its own special way.
keyPoints: Land is a natural resource of utmost importance.
Land supports vegetation, wild life, human life, work, transport and communication.
Land is limited, so careful planning is needed.
activities.explanation: Land gives us almost everything we need, but there is only so much of it.

activities.prompt: Our town built new houses and a road on old farm fields. My uncle says we can always find more land later. Is he right?
steps: Land is a natural resource of utmost importance, so losing it matters a lot.
The same land supports vegetation, wild life, people, work, transport and communication, so many needs compete for it.
Land is an asset of finite magnitude, so the Earth cannot make more of it for us.
So my uncle is wrong; we need careful planning before using up farmland.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Land Is Used
activities.body: Not all land is used in the same way. Some land is under forests. Some is barren or covered by buildings, roads and factories, so crops cannot grow there. Some land is left without cultivation for a year — this is current fallow. And some land is sown with crops, once or even more than once in a year.
keyPoints: Land use includes forests, unusable land, other uncultivated land, fallow land and net sown area.
Land for buildings, roads and factories is a non-agricultural use.
Current fallow is left without cultivation for one or less than one agricultural year.
activities.explanation: Every piece of land has a job — some grows trees, some grows crops, and some carries our roads and homes.

activities.prompt: Why should we plan how we use land?
options: Because land is limited in size
Because land grows bigger each year
Because land is found everywhere
Because land is very cheap to buy
activities.explanation: Land is an asset of finite magnitude. It cannot grow, so we must use it wisely.

activities.prompt: Barren and waste land can easily be used for growing crops.
activities.explanation: Barren and waste land is land not available for cultivation. That is why it stays unploughed.

activities.prompt: Mountains cover 30 per cent of India's surface. What special gift do they give us?
options: They ensure perennial flow of some rivers
They provide the richest mineral reserves
They offer the best land for factories
They hold most of the net sown area
activities.explanation: Mountains ensure that some rivers flow all year round. Minerals are the gift of the plateau, not the mountains.

activities.prompt: Match each land form with what it gives us.
activities.explanation: Each kind of land has its own use. Plains feed us, mountains feed our rivers, and plateaus hide treasure below the ground.

activities.prompt: Gross cropped area is net sown area plus the area sown more than ______ in an agricultural year.
activities.hint: Think of a field that grows two crops in the same year.
activities.explanation: When a field is sown more than once, it is counted again in the gross cropped area.

activities.prompt: Put the ways land resources are used in the order given in your book.
items: Forests
Land not available for cultivation
Other uncultivated land
Fallow lands
Net sown area
activities.explanation: This is the list of land uses from your lesson, from forests right through to the net sown area.

activities.prompt: Punjab has wide flat plains. Arunachal Pradesh has steep mountains. Farmers sow crops on over 80 per cent of land in Punjab. Why do farmers in Arunachal sow on less than 10 per cent?
options: Because steep mountains leave very little flat land for crops.
Because people there do not like farming at all.
Because mountains have no soil anywhere on them.
Because the government has banned farming in hills.

why.Because people there do not like farming: This blames people's choices, but land use is decided by physical factors like topography.
why.Because mountains have no soil anywhere: This goes too far; the fact says relief, not total lack of soil, limits farming.
why.Because the government has banned farmin: No ban is given; the difference is explained by the land's relief features.

activities.explanation: Right: plains give facilities for agriculture, but steep relief does not, so net sown area stays tiny.

activities.prompt: One field was left without cultivation for one agricultural year. Another field is barren and waste land. A road runs on a third field. Which land can the farmer sow again next year?
options: The road, because roads can easily change.
The waste land, because it is lying empty.
The current fallow, because it was left uncultivated for one year only.
None of them, because empty land is always barren.

why.The road, because roads can easily chang: Roads are put to non-agricultural uses, so crops cannot be sown there.
why.The waste land, because it is lying empt: Empty-looking is not enough; waste land is not available for cultivation.
why.None of them, because empty land is alwa: This confuses all empty land; fallow land is empty but still cultivable.

activities.explanation: Right: current fallow is left without cultivation for one or less than one agricultural year, so it can be sown again.

activities.prompt: A farmer owns 2 hectares of land. He grows rice on both hectares. In the same year, he grows wheat on the same 2 hectares again. What is his gross cropped area?
options: 2 hectares, because he owns only 2 hectares of land.
4 hectares, because the same land was sown more than once.
1 hectare, because wheat simply replaced the rice.
0 hectares, because the rice was already harvested.

why.2 hectares, because he owns only 2 hecta: This confuses net sown area with gross cropped area; sowing twice counts again.
why.1 hectare, because wheat simply replaced: The second crop does not replace the first; it is added to the total.
why.0 hectares, because the rice was already: Harvesting rice does not erase the sowing; both sowings are counted.

activities.explanation: Right: gross cropped area is net sown area plus the area sown more than once, so 2 plus 2 makes 4.

activities.prompt: A town keeps growing. Builders turn old farm fields into houses, roads and factories. Planners study the map with worry. Why do the planners worry so much?
options: Because land is finite, so farmland lost to buildings never comes back.
Because rain will wash all the town's land away.
Because new land grows a little every single year.
Because buildings can be shifted to make farms again.

why.Because rain will wash all the town's la: Washing away is not the issue; the issue is land being finite.
why.Because new land grows a little every si: The Earth cannot grow new land; that is why planning is needed.
why.Because buildings can be shifted to make: Buildings and roads are not easily undone; planners cannot count on that.

activities.explanation: Right: land is an asset of finite magnitude, so land put to non-agricultural uses is lost for cultivation without careful planning.

lessons.title: Land Degradation and Soil as a Resource

activities.prompt: Why does it take millions of years to make just a few centimetres of soil?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Soil and Land Matter
activities.body: Soil is the most important natural resource. It is the medium of plant growth and supports different living organisms. But soil takes millions of years to form even a few centimetres in depth. When we use land again and again without caring for it, the land gets worn out. This is called land degradation, and it hurts both people and nature.
keyPoints: Soil is the most important natural resource.
Soil takes millions of years to form a few centimetres.
Using land without conservation causes land degradation.
activities.explanation: Soil grows our food, so we must protect it.

activities.prompt: Ravi's village uses the same land year after year, but nobody looks after it. What problem can this cause?
options: Land degradation
Soil formation
Afforestation
activities.explanation: Continuous use of land without conservation and management causes land degradation. Caring for land keeps it healthy.

activities.prompt: Soil is the most important natural resource.
activities.explanation: Yes! Soil is the medium of plant growth and supports different living organisms. That makes it precious.

activities.prompt: Soil takes ______ of years to form up to a few cm in depth.
activities.hint: Think of a very, very long time — longer than a thousand years!
activities.explanation: Soil forms very slowly, over millions of years. That is why we must not waste it.

activities.prompt: Match each region with the main cause of its land degradation.
activities.explanation: Different problems harm land in different places. Mining causes deforestation in Jharkhand, overgrazing in Gujarat, and over irrigation in Punjab.

activities.prompt: What is left behind at a mining site after excavation?
options: Deep scars and over-burdening
Fresh green forests
Shelter belts of trees
activities.explanation: Mining sites are abandoned after excavation, leaving deep scars and over-burdening. The land is left damaged.

activities.prompt: Overgrazing is a main reason for land degradation in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
activities.explanation: In those places, over irrigation causes water logging, salinity and alkalinity. Overgrazing is a main reason in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of how soil forms and serves life in order.
items: Parent rock, climate and vegetation shape the ground
Forces of nature like running water and wind act on it over time
Soil forms a few cm deep after millions of years
Soil supports plants and other living organisms
activities.explanation: Soil forms slowly from parent rock, helped by forces of nature. Once formed, it supports plant growth and living organisms.

activities.prompt: A village in a dry, arid area wants to check land degradation. Which plan matches the lesson?
options: Plant shelter belts and stabilise sand dunes with thorny bushes
Abandon the land and dig new mines nearby
Use more irrigation water on the same fields
activities.explanation: Planting shelter belts, controlling overgrazing and stabilising sand dunes with thorny bushes check land degradation in arid areas.

lessons.title: Soil Types and Soil Erosion

activities.prompt: Why do farmers in some regions grow cotton while others grow rice?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Soils of India
activities.body: India has many kinds of soil. Alluvial soil is the most widely spread and important. It is a mix of sand, silt and clay. Black soil holds moisture and is ideal for cotton. Red, laterite and arid soils grow in special climates. Sometimes water washes the soil away. This is called soil erosion. Farmers can slow it with clever ploughing and terraces.
keyPoints: Alluvial soil is the most widely spread and important soil.
Black soil is ideal for cotton and holds moisture.
Soil erosion is when water washes the soil cover away.
activities.explanation: Different soils suit different crops and climates, and water can wash soil away.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants to grow cotton. Which soil should she choose?
options: Arid soil
Black soil
Red soil
activities.explanation: Black soil is ideal for growing cotton. It holds moisture well.

activities.prompt: Alluvial soil is the most widely spread and important soil.
activities.explanation: Well done! Alluvial soil covers the largest area and matters the most.

activities.prompt: Old alluvial soil has a special name in your book. It is called ______.
activities.hint: It starts with B, like the old banks of a river.
activities.explanation: Old alluvial soil is called Bangar. New alluvial soil is called Khadar.

activities.prompt: Match each soil with its special feature.
pairs: Mix of sand, silt and clay
Grows on igneous rocks in low rainfall
activities.explanation: Each soil has its own mix and its own home. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Terrace cultivation makes soil erosion worse.
activities.explanation: The opposite is true! Terrace cultivation restricts erosion and protects the soil.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of soil erosion by running water in order.
items: The soil cover is worn away
Water washes the loose soil down
Deep channels called gullies form
activities.explanation: First the cover is denuded, then water washes it down, and gullies make bad land.

activities.prompt: Why does contour ploughing protect the soil on a hillside?
options: It decelerates water flowing down the slope
It makes the soil more sandy
It adds new alluvial soil called Khadar
activities.explanation: Ploughing along the slope slows the water down, so it carries away less soil.

activities.context: In a hill village, a stream flows past the fields. For years nobody touched it. Then the panchayat bought pumps, trained young people to run them, and made rules so every family gets water on fixed days. The water now supplies homes and a small vegetable business. The elders say the stream was always there, but it became useful only when people learned to use it together.
activities.prompt: Why did the stream become a resource for the village only after the pumps and rules came?
options: Because flowing water is always counted as a resource wherever it is found
Because it became technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable to use it
Because nature had finally decided to gift the water to the village
Because the stream changed from a non-renewable to a renewable resource

why.Because flowing water is always counted: Wrong: a thing in the environment is not automatically a resource; conditions must be met.
why.Because nature had finally decided to gi: Wrong: resources are not free gifts of nature; human effort made the stream useful.
why.Because the stream changed from a non-re: Wrong: exhaustibility is about whether the resource runs out, not about whether people start using it.

activities.explanation: Correct: the pumps made it accessible, the business made it feasible, and the village accepted the sharing rules.

activities.context: In a hill village, a stream flows past the fields. For years nobody touched it. Then the panchayat bought pumps, trained young people to run them, and made rules so every family gets water on fixed days. The water now supplies homes and a small vegetable business. The elders say the stream was always there, but it became useful only when people learned to use it together.
activities.prompt: Suppose the pumps break down and no one in the village knows how to repair them. What is the most likely result?
options: The stream will stop flowing, since it depended on the pumps
The stream will instantly become an international resource for other villages
The stream will remain in the environment but stop working as a resource for the village
The water will turn non-renewable because it is no longer being used

why.The stream will stop flowing, since it d: Wrong: the stream flows on its own; only its use depended on the pumps.
why.The stream will instantly become an inte: Wrong: ownership does not change just because a village stops using a resource.
why.The water will turn non-renewable becaus: Wrong: whether water is renewable depends on its nature, not on whether people currently use it.

activities.explanation: Correct: without the technology to draw the water, it is back to being just a thing in the environment, not a resource.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Human beings are essential components of resources.
Reason (R): Human beings transform the materials available in the environment into resources and use them.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains the assertion, since it is people's transforming activity that makes humans essential to resources.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Resources are free gifts of nature.
Reason (R): A thing in the environment becomes a resource only when it can satisfy a human need.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because resources require human effort and conditions, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why resources are not free gifts of nature.
activities.answer: A thing in the environment becomes a resource only when it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable. These conditions are created by human beings, not by nature. People interact with nature through technology and create institutions to speed up economic development, transforming materials into useful resources. Since human effort, skill and organisation are needed before anything can satisfy our needs, resources are the result of human activities rather than ready-made gifts.
points: States the three conditions: technologically accessible, economically feasible, culturally acceptable
Says these conditions are created by human beings, not by nature
Mentions interaction of nature, technology and institutions
Concludes that resources are a function of human activities
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The town of Rampur grew fast because its factories cut down nearby forests and used river water freely, believing nature's supplies would never run out. Soon wells dried up, fish died, and a few rich owners grew richer while most villagers lost their livelihoods. The town council now wants to follow the spirit of the 1992 Rio meeting and prepare its own plan for development that protects the environment.
activities.prompt: If Rampur's council writes a plan in the spirit of Agenda 21, what should it most likely do?
options: Ask the national government to write the whole plan for the town
Prepare a local plan balancing development with protection of forests and water
Allow factory owners to expand since they create the most wealth
Ban all factories immediately so nature can recover on its own

why.Ask the national government to write the: Agenda 21 expects each local government to draw up its own plan, not wait for the centre
why.Allow factory owners to expand since the: This repeats the greed of a few that caused the crisis in the first place
why.Ban all factories immediately so nature: An extreme step; sustainability is about balance, not stopping all development

activities.explanation: Correct: sustainable development means meeting needs without damaging the environment or future generations

activities.context: The town of Rampur grew fast because its factories cut down nearby forests and used river water freely, believing nature's supplies would never run out. Soon wells dried up, fish died, and a few rich owners grew richer while most villagers lost their livelihoods. The town council now wants to follow the spirit of the 1992 Rio meeting and prepare its own plan for development that protects the environment.
activities.prompt: Why did the wells in Rampur dry up and the fish die?
options: Because the council never signed any international declaration
Because future generations moved away from the town
Because resources were used carelessly as if they were free and unlimited
Because the rich owners shared their wealth too widely

why.Because the council never signed any int: Signing a declaration is a step taken at summits; the damage came from local overuse
why.Because future generations moved away fr: Future generations were affected by the damage, not the cause of it
why.Because the rich owners shared their wea: The opposite happened; accumulation in a few hands divided society, it did not cause plenty

activities.explanation: Correct: indiscriminate use of resources, seen as free gifts of nature, caused the ecological crisis

activities.context: The town of Rampur grew fast because its factories cut down nearby forests and used river water freely, believing nature's supplies would never run out. Soon wells dried up, fish died, and a few rich owners grew richer while most villagers lost their livelihoods. The town council now wants to follow the spirit of the 1992 Rio meeting and prepare its own plan for development that protects the environment.
activities.prompt: If Rampur continues its present pattern of use for another twenty years, what is the most likely outcome?
options: The gap between rich owners and villagers will shrink on its own
Resources will keep renewing themselves no matter how they are used
Environmental damage will deepen and the needs of future townspeople will be at risk
Only the villagers will suffer while the environment stays untouched

why.The gap between rich owners and villager: Accumulation in few hands has already divided society; nothing suggests it will shrink by itself
why.Resources will keep renewing themselves: The case shows resources deplete when used indiscriminately
why.Only the villagers will suffer while the: Ecological crises affect everyone who depends on resources, not only one group

activities.explanation: Correct: development that damages the environment compromises the needs of future generations

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The first International Earth Summit was attended by more than 100 heads of states.
Reason (R): The summit was held in Rio de Janeiro in June 1992.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the location and timing do not explain the large attendance.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Society got divided into haves and have nots because resources came to be accumulated in a few hands.
Reason (R): Agenda 21 was adopted to divide society into rich and poor sections.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but Agenda 21 aims at achieving global sustainable development, not dividing society.

activities.prompt: Explain why the indiscriminate use of resources, once thought to be free gifts of nature, led to both social and global problems.
activities.answer: People once believed that resources were free gifts of nature, so they used them indiscriminately to satisfy the greed of a few individuals. This led to the depletion of resources. As resources accumulated in the hands of a few, society got divided into haves and have nots, creating inequality. At the same time, the indiscriminate exploitation of resources caused global ecological crises, showing that development which damages the environment cannot last and harms future generations too.
points: Belief that resources were free gifts led to indiscriminate use
Depletion occurred to satisfy the greed of a few
Accumulation in few hands divided society into haves and have nots
Indiscriminate exploitation led to global ecological crises
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a field visit, students compare two regions. In the first, farmers grow crops on almost every plot, and very little land is left for anything else. In the second, a hilly region, only a tiny fraction of the land is sown, while steep slopes remain under forest. The students also learn that the country's land is fixed in extent, so every new road or building takes land away from some other use.
activities.prompt: If a large factory is built on farmland in the first region, what will most likely happen to the land under crops there?
options: It will shrink, because land occupied by buildings cannot simultaneously grow crops
It will expand, because factories make nearby fields more productive
It will stay the same, because one plot can serve farming and industry at once
It will be counted twice, first as farmland and then as industrial land

why.It will expand, because factories make n: Wrong: industrial growth does not create extra farmland; the land itself is lost to crops.
why.It will stay the same, because one plot: Wrong: a single piece of land cannot be under a factory and under crops at the same time.
why.It will be counted twice, first as farml: Wrong: double counting applies to repeated sowing of crops, not to land diverted to factories.

activities.explanation: Correct: land is fixed in extent, so non-agricultural use directly replaces cultivation.

activities.context: During a field visit, students compare two regions. In the first, farmers grow crops on almost every plot, and very little land is left for anything else. In the second, a hilly region, only a tiny fraction of the land is sown, while steep slopes remain under forest. The students also learn that the country's land is fixed in extent, so every new road or building takes land away from some other use.
activities.prompt: Why is only a tiny fraction of land sown in the hilly region the students visited?
options: The relief of the area leaves most of its surface unsuitable for sowing crops
The farmers there deliberately keep all their fields as current fallow every year
Most of the fields have been taken over for buildings, roads and factories
The land there is sown more than once, so less of it needs to be used

why.The farmers there deliberately keep all: Wrong: current fallow means land rested for one agricultural year or less, not an entire region unsown.
why.Most of the fields have been taken over: Wrong: the passage says slopes remain under forest, not that non-agricultural uses have spread there.
why.The land there is sown more than once, s: Wrong: sowing more than once raises gross cropped area; it does not reduce the extent of land sown.

activities.explanation: Correct: topography is a physical factor, and steep mountainous relief limits the land available for cultivation.

activities.context: During a field visit, students compare two regions. In the first, farmers grow crops on almost every plot, and very little land is left for anything else. In the second, a hilly region, only a tiny fraction of the land is sown, while steep slopes remain under forest. The students also learn that the country's land is fixed in extent, so every new road or building takes land away from some other use.
activities.prompt: The village panchayat in the first region wants a new road but some fields would have to be given up. Since the total land cannot be increased, what should the panchayat do first?
options: Carefully work out how much land the road truly needs and which existing use it will displace
Acquire as much land as possible, since more land can always be found later
Record the land taken for the road as current fallow so no cultivation is shown as lost
Shift the road to the hilly region, where plenty of unused plain land is available

why.Acquire as much land as possible, since: Wrong: land cannot be expanded, so taking extra land wastefully is not a solution.
why.Record the land taken for the road as cu: Wrong: fallow land is cultivable land rested temporarily; a road is a permanent non-agricultural use.
why.Shift the road to the hilly region, wher: Wrong: the hilly region has little sown land because of its relief; it does not offer spare plain land.

activities.explanation: Correct: because land is fixed in extent, its diversion demands careful planning of competing uses.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Mountains are valuable to India's river system.
Reason (R): Mountains ensure the perennial flow of some rivers.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the perennial flow they ensure is exactly why mountains are valuable to the river system.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Land use data in India is available for the country's entire geographical area.
Reason (R): The total geographical area of India is 3.28 million sq km.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because data covers only 93 per cent of the area, while the reason stating the total area is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why careful planning of land use is necessary in India.
activities.answer: Land is a natural resource of utmost importance because it supports natural vegetation, wild life, human life, economic activities, and transport and communication. Since land is an asset of finite magnitude, its extent cannot be increased, so land given to one use, such as buildings or roads, is taken away from another, like cultivation or forests. India's forest area is already far lower than the desired 33 per cent of the geographical area. Hence, careful planning is needed so that today's competing demands do not rob future generations of this resource.
points: Land supports vegetation, wild life, human life, economic activities, transport and communication
Land is of finite magnitude, so it cannot be expanded
One use gained means another use lost, creating competing demands
Forest area is far below the desired 33 per cent, so planning must protect it
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: A thing in our environment becomes a resource only when it meets three conditions. Which set is correct?
options: Technologically accessible, economically feasible, culturally acceptable
Technologically new, economically costly, culturally famous
Technologically old, economically free, culturally ancient
activities.explanation: Well done! A thing must be usable with our technology, worth the cost, and accepted by people to count as a resource.

activities.prompt: Resources are free gifts of nature, so we may use them in any way we like.
activities.explanation: Resources are not free gifts of nature. People once believed this and used them carelessly, which caused great harm.

activities.prompt: Match each soil with its special feature.
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each soil has its own story, from cotton fields to desert sands.

activities.prompt: In June ______, more than 100 heads of states met in Rio de Janeiro for the first International Earth Summit.
activities.hint: It was the last year of the 1980s plus two.
activities.explanation: Yes! The leaders met in 1992 to discuss protecting the environment and development together.

activities.prompt: A village pond is used by everyone in the village. On the basis of ownership, how is this resource classified?
options: Community resource
Individual resource
International resource
activities.explanation: Well done! Resources owned by a whole community, like a pond, are community resources.

activities.prompt: Put the parts of resource planning in the correct order, starting with the first step.
items: Identify and make an inventory of resources across regions
Survey, map and estimate the resources
Evolve a planning structure with technology, skill and institutions
Match resource development plans with national development plans
activities.explanation: Perfect order! First we find and measure resources, then build the plan, then join it with national plans.

activities.prompt: Gross cropped area is the net sown area plus the area sown more than once in an agricultural year.
activities.explanation: Correct! When farmers grow a second crop on the same land, that area is added to get gross cropped area.

activities.prompt: In Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, farmers use too much water on their fields. What problem does this over irrigation cause?
options: Water logging, salinity and alkalinity
Deep scars and over-burdening
Alternate wet and dry seasons
activities.explanation: Yes! Too much irrigation water logs the fields and makes the soil salty and alkaline.

activities.prompt: Ploughing along the contour lines on a slope ______ the flow of water down the slope, so the soil is washed away more slowly.
activities.explanation: Well done! Contour ploughing slows the water down, giving it less power to carry the soil away.

activities.prompt: Agenda 21 was adopted at the Rio Summit. What is one major objective of Agenda 21?
options: Every local government should draw its own local Agenda 21
Every country should stop all farming to save soil
Every family should move to a mountain region
activities.explanation: Correct! Agenda 21 aims at global sustainable development, and each local government draws up its own local plan for it.

lessons.title: Flora and Fauna in India

activities.prompt: Why should we care about the plants and animals around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: We Share Our Planet
activities.body: You share this planet with millions of other living beings. Our habitat has immense biodiversity, which means many kinds of plants and animals live here. Humans and all living organisms form a complex web of ecological system. Humans are only a part of this web, and we depend on it very much.
keyPoints: Millions of living beings share our planet.
Humans and other organisms form one web of life.
Humans are part of this web and depend on it.
activities.explanation: Nature is one big family, and you are a member of it.

activities.prompt: A farmer cuts all the trees on his hill to grow more crops. Next year, his well has less water and the soil is weak. Why did this happen?
steps: Trees are plants, and plants are the primary producers in nature, so everything else depends on them.
When the trees go, the web of living things on the hill breaks, because all beings are closely integrated.
Plants help re-create the quality of soil and water, so without them the soil becomes weak and water sinks in less.
So the farmer lost his crops' support system, because humans are only a part of the system and depend on it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which of these plays a key role in the ecological system as primary producers?
options: Rivers and lakes
Forests
Deserts
Mountains
activities.explanation: Well done! Forests are the primary producers, so they start the food chain for everyone.

activities.prompt: India is one of the world's richest countries in biological ______.
activities.hint: It means the variety of living things.
activities.explanation: Great job! India is among the richest countries in biological diversity.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: Super matching! You have linked each part of nature to its role.

activities.prompt: Why do all other living beings depend on forests?
options: Because forests are primary producers
Because forests are fun to visit
Because forests are far from cities
Because forests are always silent
activities.explanation: Correct! As primary producers, forests support every other living being in the web.

activities.prompt: Put these ideas in order, starting with who makes food for the web.
items: Forests act as primary producers.
All other living beings depend on the primary producers.
Humans depend on this system as a part of the web.
activities.explanation: Perfect order! Food and support flow from the producers to all living beings, including you.

activities.prompt: Biodiversity is immensely rich in which two kinds of species?
options: Wildlife and cultivated species
Pets and wild weeds
Birds and fishes only
Crops and insects only
activities.explanation: Well done! Biodiversity is rich in both wildlife and cultivated species, and they all work closely together.

activities.prompt: Ravi says humans are the masters of nature, so nothing depends on other living beings. His friend Meena disagrees. Who is right, and why?
options: Meena, because all living beings form one linked web
Ravi, because humans are the biggest part of the web
Meena, because India has very rich biological diversity
Ravi, because humans can re-create air and water alone

why.Ravi, because humans are the biggest par: This thinks humans stand above the web, but we are only a part of it.
why.Meena, because India has very rich biolo: This is true about India, but it does not answer whether humans depend on other beings.
why.Ravi, because humans can re-create air a: This thinks humans work alone, but plants and micro-organisms also re-create air and water.

activities.explanation: Right: humans and all organisms form one complex web, so we depend on other beings.

activities.prompt: Two islands are the same size. Island A lost its plants. Island B kept its plants. Which island will keep more animals alive, and why?
options: Island B, because animals depend on primary producers
Island A, because fewer plants means more space for animals
Island B, because its species are diverse in form
Island A, because animals can re-create their own food

why.Island A, because fewer plants means mor: This thinks space matters most, but animals need plants as the base of the system.
why.Island B, because its species are divers: This is true of Island B, but the real reason is that plants are primary producers.
why.Island A, because animals can re-create: This thinks animals make their own food, but only primary producers do that.

activities.explanation: Right: all other living beings depend on primary producers, so plants keep animals alive.

activities.prompt: A student says wildlife and farm crops are separate worlds with no link. What is wrong with her thinking?
options: Wildlife and cultivated species are closely integrated
Cultivated species are always stronger than wildlife
Wildlife can live well without any cultivated species
Farm crops are not part of biodiversity at all

why.Cultivated species are always stronger t: This thinks one kind is stronger, but the fact says they are linked, not ranked.
why.Wildlife can live well without any culti: This thinks the two are separate, but they are closely integrated in one system.
why.Farm crops are not part of biodiversity: This thinks farms are outside nature, but cultivated species are part of biodiversity.

activities.explanation: Right: biodiversity is rich in wildlife and cultivated species, and species are closely integrated.

activities.prompt: A city sprays poison that kills micro-organisms in the soil. Farmers there must buy more fertiliser every year. What is the best reason for this?
options: Micro-organisms help re-create the quality of the soil
Farmers always need more fertiliser every single year
The poison made the city's air much cleaner instead
Soil quality never changes, whatever happens to it

why.Farmers always need more fertiliser ever: This thinks fertiliser use is a habit, not a result of losing soil quality.
why.The poison made the city's air much clea: This talks about air, but the problem here is about soil quality.
why.Soil quality never changes, whatever hap: This thinks soil stays the same, but living beings keep re-creating its quality.

activities.explanation: Right: micro-organisms re-create the quality of soil, so killing them harms the soil.

activities.prompt: A boy finds one rare plant near his town and says, 'Losing one species is fine, the rest will stay the same.' What should his teacher say?
options: No, species are closely integrated in one system
Yes, because millions of other beings still remain
Yes, because plants are only a small part of life
No, because India is the richest country in diversity

why.Yes, because millions of other beings st: This thinks big numbers protect the system, but the links between species matter too.
why.Yes, because plants are only a small par: This thinks plants matter little, but forests are primary producers that all beings depend on.
why.No, because India is the richest country: This is true about India, but it does not explain why one lost species matters.

activities.explanation: Right: species are diverse but closely integrated, so losing one affects the whole web.

lessons.title: Conservation of Forest and Wildlife in India

activities.prompt: What happens to us if India's forests and wild animals keep disappearing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why do we conserve forests and wildlife?
activities.body: Wildlife and forests were declining fast, so conservation became essential. It protects ecological diversity and the systems that keep life going. It also saves the genetic variety of plants and animals, which helps them grow and breed well. In the 1960s and 1970s, conservationists asked for a national wildlife protection programme.
keyPoints: Conservation became essential because wildlife and forests declined rapidly.
It preserves ecological diversity and life support systems.
It protects genetic diversity for better growth and breeding.
activities.explanation: Protecting nature keeps life on Earth healthy for everyone.

activities.prompt: A village pond has many kinds of fish and water plants. One year, the water plants die. Soon the fish catch becomes very small. Why did this happen?
steps: The fish in the pond depend on the water plants for food and shelter.
When the plants die, the fish lose their life support in the pond.
So fewer fish survive, and the fishermen catch much less.
This shows that fisheries depend on the many kinds of living things in water.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why did conservation become essential in India?
options: Because wildlife and forests declined rapidly
Because forests grew too quickly
Because there were too many parks
activities.explanation: Well done! Wildlife and forestry fell fast, so saving them became vital.

activities.prompt: In the 1960s and 1970s, conservationists demanded a national wildlife ______ programme.
activities.hint: It is the word for keeping something safe from harm.
activities.explanation: Great! Conservationists asked for a national wildlife protection programme.

activities.prompt: Match each need with what it depends on.
pairs: Genetic diversity of plants and animals
activities.explanation: Super! Farms, fisheries and breeding all depend on different kinds of diversity.

activities.prompt: What did the wildlife protection programme do to save endangered species?

Encouraged hunting in forests
Sold endangered animals abroad

activities.prompt: An all-India list of ______ species was published.

activities.explanation: Well done! The list told everyone which species were protected.

activities.prompt: Put these steps of the protection programme in order.
items: Conservationists demanded a national wildlife protection programme
An all-India list of protected species was published
Central and state governments set up national parks and wildlife sanctuaries
activities.explanation: Great thinking! First came the demand, then the list, then the parks and sanctuaries.

activities.prompt: A pond has many kinds of water plants and fish. The plants die. Then the fish catch gets smaller. Why did the fish catch get smaller?
options: The fish lost their food and homes when the plants died.
The fish all swam away to another pond far off.
The pond water became too deep for fish to swim.
The fishermen became lazy and stopped going to the pond.

why.The fish all swam away to another pond f: This blames a random escape, not the loss of the fish's life support.
why.The pond water became too deep for fish: This blames a change in water depth, which the story never says.
why.The fishermen became lazy and stopped go: This blames the people instead of the broken web of water life.

activities.explanation: Right. Water life depends on many living things staying healthy together.

activities.prompt: India has one list of protected animals for the whole country. A man sees a rare bird from this list in his field. He wants to shoot it. Why can he not shoot it?
options: Hunting protected animals is banned so rare ones can survive.
The bird is too small, so a gun cannot hit it well.
The bird belongs to his neighbour, so it is not his.
Shooting birds is allowed only on some days of the year.

why.The bird is too small, so a gun cannot h: This thinks size matters, but the rule is about protection, not size.
why.The bird belongs to his neighbour, so it: This thinks ownership is the reason, not the protection law.
why.Shooting birds is allowed only on some d: This thinks the ban is only for some days, not a full ban.

activities.explanation: Right. The ban on hunting protects endangered listed species.

activities.prompt: A farmer grows his family's old rice seeds. He also grows new rice seeds. Why does he keep the old seeds too?
options: Old seeds keep many plant types for better breeding later.
Old seeds always grow faster than any new seed can.
Old seeds need no water, so they save him much work.
Old seeds look pretty, so shops pay him more money.

why.Old seeds always grow faster than any ne: This thinks old seeds are simply better growers, which is not the reason.
why.Old seeds need no water, so they save hi: This adds a magic power the old seeds do not really have.
why.Old seeds look pretty, so shops pay him: This thinks the reason is money from looks, not saving plant variety.

activities.prompt: A big forest stands near a village. The forest is cut down. After some years, the village springs give less water. Why did the springs give less water?

The villagers used the spring water to wash too many clothes.
The springs moved underground because they did not like the village.
The sun drank all the spring water in that one year.

why.The villagers used the spring water to w: This blames the villagers' washing, not the loss of the forest.
why.The springs moved underground because th: This gives springs feelings and a choice, which they do not have.
why.The sun drank all the spring water in th: This blames one hot year, but the change came after the forest fell.

activities.explanation: Right. Forests are life support systems, so losing them harms water too.

activities.prompt: How did India bring its tigers back from the edge of disappearing?

activities.title: Why we save the tiger
activities.body: The tiger is a key species in the faunal web, the web of animal life in a forest. Long ago there were about 55,000 tigers, but by 1973 only 1,827 were left. Poaching, shrinking habitat and loss of prey hurt them. So India started Project Tiger in 1973 to protect tigers and the large wild places they live in.
keyPoints: The tiger is a key species in the faunal web.
Tiger numbers fell from 55,000 to 1,827 by 1973.
Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect tigers and their homes.

Poaching and shrinking habitat

activities.prompt: India and Nepal became prime targets for poaching and illegal trading because they hold about two-thirds of surviving tigers.

Tiger count falls to 1,827 in 1973
Project Tiger is launched in 1973

lessons.title: Types and Distribution of Forest and Wildlife Resources

activities.prompt: Who really owns India's forests, and how are they sorted?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Three Kinds of Forests
activities.body: Forests and wildlife are hard to manage and look after. Much of them is owned or managed by the government. To make this easier, forests are sorted into categories. Reserved forests are the biggest group and are most valuable for conservation. Protected forests are kept safe from further loss. Unclassed forests are other forests and wastelands.
keyPoints: Forest and wildlife resources are hard to manage and control.
Much forest land is owned or managed by the government.
Forests are grouped as reserved, protected and unclassified.
activities.explanation: Sorting forests into groups helps the government look after them better.

activities.prompt: Which category covers more than half of the total forest land?
options: Reserved forests
Protected forests
Unclassed forests
activities.explanation: Well done! Reserved forests take up more than half of all forest land.

activities.prompt: Almost one-third of the total forest area is protected forest.
activities.explanation: Yes! Protected forests make up almost one-third of the forest area.

activities.prompt: The state with the largest area under permanent forests is ______.
activities.hint: A large state in the middle of India.
activities.explanation: Great! Madhya Pradesh has the largest area under permanent forests.

activities.prompt: Match each forest category with what it means.
pairs: More than half of forest land
activities.explanation: Each category covers a different share and kind of forest land.

activities.prompt: Why are reserved forests so special?
options: They are most valuable for conservation
They are wastelands of private people
They are the newest forests in India
activities.explanation: Reserved forests are the most valuable ones for conservation of nature.

activities.prompt: Unclassed forests belong only to the government.
activities.explanation: Not quite! Unclassed forests belong to the government, private people and communities.

activities.prompt: Put these categories in order, from the most carefully guarded to the least.

Protected forests

activities.explanation: Reserved forests are most valuable for conservation, then protected forests, then unclassified ones.

options: It will not be used up and lost any more
It will be given to private people to own
It will be counted as unclassified forest
activities.explanation: Depletion means loss. Protected forests are kept safe so they are not used up further.

activities.prompt: Can ordinary villagers really protect forests better than anyone else?

activities.title: People Who Protect Nature
activities.body: Saving forests is not new in India. Some traditional communities live in forests and know them well. When their homes and livelihoods are at risk, local people fight to protect them. They struggle with officials so that habitats stay safe for the long term.
keyPoints: Conservation strategies are not new in India.
Forests are home to some traditional communities.
Local communities work to conserve habitats for their long-term livelihood.
activities.explanation: People who live closest to nature often care for it the most.

A new village school

A ban on all farming

activities.title: Sonchuri Check

activities.explanation: Yes! Five villages set aside 1,200 hectares and called it Sonchuri.

activities.title: Rules of the Forest
activities.prompt: The villagers of Sonchuri made rules that do not allow ______ and protect wildlife from encroachments.
activities.hint: What activity with animals did the villagers stop?
activities.explanation: The rules ban hunting so that wildlife stays safe. Well done!

activities.title: Who Did What?

activities.body: In many areas, villagers protect habitats on their own and say no to government help. The Chipko movement resisted deforestation and proved that communities can grow forests too. When people plant and guard trees together, this is called community afforestation, and it can succeed.

Mining in forests
Hunting of wildlife

activities.title: Farming Without Chemicals

Illegal

lessons.title: Sacred Groves and Nature Worship

activities.prompt: Why would people leave a whole forest completely untouched for centuries?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Forests Kept Safe by Faith
activities.body: Long ago, tribal people believed that every part of nature must be protected. This belief is called nature worship. Because of it, some forest patches were left untouched by local people. These green patches stayed wild and pure. They are called Sacred Groves, the forests of God and Goddesses. Nobody is allowed to harm them.
keyPoints: Nature worship says all creations of nature must be protected.
Sacred Groves are virgin forests kept in pristine form.
Local people left these forest patches untouched.
Any interference with Sacred Groves is banned.
activities.explanation: Faith helped keep whole forests safe and wild.

activities.prompt: What is a Sacred Grove?
options: A garden made by a king
A forest patch left untouched by local people
A farm where trees are planted in rows
A park with swings and slides
activities.explanation: Sacred Groves are forest patches people left untouched out of belief. Well done!

activities.prompt: Sacred Groves are called the forests of God and Goddesses.
activities.explanation: Yes! People saw these forests as holy homes of the divine.

activities.prompt: The Mundas and Santhal worship the ______ tree and the kadamba tree.

activities.prompt: Which pair of trees is considered sacred?

Mahua and kadamba
Peepal and banyan
Kadamba and mango

activities.prompt: People may cut trees freely inside a Sacred Grove.

activities.prompt: Match each group or place with the trees it worships.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how a Sacred Grove is formed.
items: People believe all creations of nature must be protected

The forest stays virgin and pristine
It is honoured as a Sacred Grove
activities.explanation: Belief comes first, then care, then a pristine forest. Lovely thinking!
